side_detail: There was more space on my right (0.67 m to the wall versus 1.08 m on my left), so moving right kept me and the suitcase clear of the oncoming person.

basis: Just common sense and courtesy: I knew her, she was pulling a large suitcase, so I gave way and gave her room to pass rather than following any formal rule.
applies_to: all the decisions: giving way politely to Person 1 and stepping aside to let her suitcase pass
side_detail: She had drifted toward my left with the suitcase, so I moved right to keep clear of it and of her.

basis: Just common courtesy and being easy-going: giving a classmate room to pass in a narrow, busy passage. No formal rule was in my mind.
applies_to: All the decisions to shift right and let my classmate pass
side_detail: My right side had less space to the wall, but stepping right kept me clear of him since he was ahead and to my left, and my suitcase trails behind me, so moving right opened the gap between us.

basis: Personal habit and stubbornness rather than any rule: as a cane user pulling a suitcase I hold my line and expect others to go around me, which is how I normally walk at home.

side_detail: The oncoming woman was drifting into my side of the passage, so moving slightly right kept me clear of her while staying near my own line; either side would have done, but she was on my left of the centre.

basis: Just common sense and courtesy: an elderly man with a cane and a large suitcase needs more room, so I gave way to the side with more space.
applies_to: all three decisions
side_detail: The wall on my right was only 0.26 m away but the left wall was 1.49 m, and he was coming slightly to my left, so shifting right gave him the wider side to pass; it was not a rule about keeping left or right.

basis: Nothing formal — I just gave way to a woman on her phone using a cane and pulling a suitcase, out of ordinary courtesy and habit rather than any rule.
applies_to: All three decisions: pacing myself and shifting aside to give Person 1 room to pass safely.

basis: Mostly common sense and habit: I keep to the right when passing someone head-on, which is the informal convention in the US and matches what I'm used to, but I was mainly reacting to where he was drifting.
applies_to: All four decisions, especially the later ones where I sidestepped right to let him pass on my left
side_detail: He was drifting toward my left, so easing right opened the gap on his side and let him pass without either of us stopping; the right also aligned with my passing-side habit.

basis: Nothing formal. I was going by personal habit and plain reactiveness after being bumped into earlier today: I wanted to keep my line and not slow down, and simply expected her to see me and go around. The sidestep plans were only ever tentative and I never actually moved aside.
applies_to: All four decisions, but especially the first three which set a sidestep or turn plan
side_detail: I never actually carried out a sidestep; the planned move to my left in the first decision was only a fallback if she got close, and my later decisions abandoned any sidestep in favour of holding my line. If I had moved, it would have been to my left because she was slightly to my left and that would have been away from her, but in the end I just kept my line.

basis: No law or guidance in mind; just everyday courtesy — giving an elderly man with a cane plenty of room, and the habit of keeping to the side of a passage. The wall on my right was close and the other person was slightly to my left, so moving right was the natural way to open a gap.
applies_to: all four decisions — giving the elderly man room and stepping to my right as we passed
side_detail: He was ahead and to my left, and my right side had the closer wall but still enough clearance, so moving right widened the gap between us; either side would have worked, but the other side was toward him.

basis: A small courtesy sidestep so we both have room to pass in a narrow passage, plus a nod of recognition to someone I know from classes; nothing formal behind it.

basis: Nothing formal, just common courtesy: she's elderly, using a cane, pulling a suitcase, and greeted me, so I nod back and give her space to pass in a narrow, busy passage.

basis: Nothing in particular beyond ordinary courtesy — giving an older person room to pass in a narrow passage, and general Singapore public-space norms of keeping left where possible; there is no specific law or study behind it.

side_detail: I stepped to my right because the wall on my right was 0.57 m away while the wall on my left was 1.18 m away, so my right side had more space to move into and opened a wider gap between us.

basis: Nothing formal; just being easy-going and giving an elderly person who was distracted by her phone plenty of clearance, and slowing down to avoid a bump.

side_detail: She was ahead and drifting toward my left, and I had more space on my own left side of the passage, so moving left put distance between us and matched where she was heading.

basis: Nothing formal — just my habit as a pedestrian and common sense: I've been knocked into once today and didn't want it again, so I stepped slightly aside while keeping my course.

basis: Just common sense: giving a wide berth to someone walking with a cane and slowing to greet a friend, plus a general habit of keeping to the left in Singapore, which put me on my right to pass her.

side_detail: She was coming toward me slightly on my left of centre, so stepping to my right opened the bigger gap and kept me toward the wall with more room.

basis: Nothing formal — just common courtesy and safety: she's elderly, using a cane and looking at her phone, so giving her plenty of room and slowing to a stop seemed the sensible, easy-going thing to do. That's how people generally behave in Singapore; there's no law or study I'm relying on.
applies_to: all of the decisions, especially the last ones (slowing, holding up a hand, stopping to let her pass)

basis: Nothing formal — just common courtesy. He's elderly, pulling a large suitcase, and nodded/said thank you, so I gave way and let him pass in the narrow passage.

side_detail: The wall on my right was only 0.25 m away, so stepping right put me close against it and left the wider remaining space (toward my left) for him and his suitcase to pass.

basis: Nothing formal—just common courtesy and my own habit of keeping well over to one side when passing someone in a narrow passage, plus slowing down to avoid a bump after being knocked into earlier.

side_detail: She was straight ahead and drifting toward my right, and the wall on my left gave me a clear, predictable margin, so moving left kept her path on my right open and put distance between us.

basis: Nothing formal — just everyday pedestrian courtesy in a narrow passage: shift a little to make room for someone coming the other way, then return to my own line to keep moving fast. In Singapore I'd generally keep left on walkways, but this was improvisation, not a rule I was following.
applies_to: the second decision: sidestepping right, then back left, to get past Person 1
side_detail: He was straight ahead coming toward me, so I chose the right to open a gap on the side I judged he was less likely to take, and I planned to slide back left afterwards to keep to the left, which is the local habit on walkways.

basis: Nothing formal — just common courtesy and easy-going habit: give an elderly person plenty of room, slow a little, and slip aside so we don't brush past each other.

basis: Just common sense about passing someone coming the other way in a narrow, busy passage while they pull a suitcase; no law, guidance, study or local custom that I know of.

side_detail: He was ahead and to my left and drifting to his right, so moving right opened up the gap between us and kept me away from the suitcase he was pulling; either side could have worked, but his position made right the easier choice.

basis: Nothing formal, just everyday common sense about not colliding in a crowded passage — matching her drift so we don't clip each other, while keeping my pace because I'm headed somewhere urgent with a suitcase.

side_detail: She was drifting to my left, so I angled that way to follow the gap she was opening rather than swing the suitcase across her path; it wasn't about a keep-left rule.
